column216: Our operator fleet consists of over 29 operators and 3 equipment specialists across 2 press series and 4 product categories. Training our entire operator fleet to Level 2 across all four press products is estimated at over $2 million. This is based on each training being valued at 8,000.00 for content and travel.  The existing training program, which requires sending operators to Alpharetta for Level 1 certification, is not sustainable for large companies investing in multiple HP Indigo technologies. A key issue is that a Level 2 certified operator on a 12K press is not certified on an 18K press, and they would need to complete both Level 1 and 2 training for each additional press type (100K and 120K).  We need a scalable and cost-effective path for operator education. This includes developing an internal training and certification program for Level 1 operators, allowing us to utilize our entitlements for advanced training more effectively. Additionally, we would like to implement "flex service" for training funds. This would allow our allocated dollars to be used à la carte and applied with greater precision to our immediate needs, rather than being tied to specific training types or values.

column116: Whatever savings may have been projected, or even realized, over the last two years can now safely be assumed to have either been taken back, or will be taken back, by HP through the new subscription and access charges that have been layered in. The bottom line is that the economics have changed, and not in my favor. I’m now looking at a model where the long-term cost of ownership is no longer predictable, and the benefits that justified the investment are being eaten away with every new policy update.  This shift doesn’t just affect numbers on a spreadsheet, it impacts how I plan, price, and grow my business. This raises a very real concern: how long until I’m back at a net loss, wondering how much more HP plans to leech from me under the guise of “platform evolution”? It’s a moving target, and it is most definitely intentional.  The strategy HP is pursuing, offering a flexible, efficient platform, then gradually locking users into recurring fees and limiting access, is the same bait-and-switch tactic I have seen utilized in other industries. The reliance on user dependence to justify changing the rules. And while it may generate short-term recurring revenue, it erodes long-term trust. This isn’t what I signed up for, and I doubt I’m alone in that feeling.  At this point, I have to seriously evaluate whether it makes more sense to walk away. For the amount of variable work I run, adding an inkjet module to my Mark Andy, or even purchasing a different, more transparent digital press supplier could very well meet my needs. On jobs under 20,000 feet, I could absorb the plate costs and still come out with a net gain by cutting ties with HP and all the newly imposed costs that now come with it.  This isn’t just about dollars it’s about control, predictability, and partnership. Right now, it’s hard to feel like HP is acting in the spirit of the agreement we entered into when I bought this press.

column136: I am extremely frustrated and disappointed with HP right now.  This latest move to transition previously included services like PrintOS into a subscription-based model is unacceptable. When I made the investment in my HP press, I was told that services like PrintOS were part of the package, not optional add-ons that could later be converted into new charges. To now see features that were once part of the value proposition being placed behind a monthly paywall feels like a bait-and-switch.  What makes this even worse is that this is now the second time this year HP has pulled something like this. HP rolling out surprise charges for services that were originally included. It’s becoming a pattern, and it’s completely eroding the trust I once had in HP as a long-term partner.  As you may know, I’m currently evaluating a replacement for my Webtron 1000. Initially, I seriously considered a new HP 8K. But then HP implemented the first round of subscription-based charges, shifting what had been a manageable, user-controlled expense into an ongoing, mandatory cost. Now, with this second bait-and-switch in such a short span, it’s impossible not to question the direction HP is heading. Why should I put my trust, and my business, in a company that continues to change the rules mid-game? Once I’m locked into a service like the Productivity Power Pack, how long will it be before the monthly fees go up again?  I understand HP has tried to justify the new charges by comparing them to the cost of a cup of coffee per day. If that’s the mindset, then I would ask, is it really worth it to HP to jeopardize the future investment of a current customer over the equivalent of a daily coffee? Because from where I stand, these approaches are not only short-sighted, they’re pushing me to engage with Mark Andy for my next press.

column148: when we purchased our HP Indigo 6K in April 2023, we were never informed that such a fundamental change to the SmartStream Designer licensing model was imminent. This information was not disclosed at the time of sale, and had it been, we would have had the opportunity to make a more informed purchasing decision—potentially even considering alternative digital printing press manufacturers.  We were not made aware of it at the time of our purchase. A mass email does not constitute proper disclosure, nor does it replace the responsibility of HP and its representatives to ensure that customers making significant financial investments are fully informed of impending structural changes to software access and costs.  This change is not just a minor price increase—it is a drastic shift in how we must operate. Under the old model, we would upgrade every 3-5 years at our discretion for a one-time cost of $1,500, averaging to around $500 per year, if we upgrade once every three years.  The reality is that our need for upgrade would fall closer to every 5 years.  This would reflect an annual cost to us of approximately $300 per year.  Under this new forced subscription model, we are now required to pay $1,800 annually—a $1,500 per year increase for the same software. Nearly a $7,500 increase in expense over the necessary upgrade timeframe.  Worse, the moment we stop paying, we lose access to the software entirely, effectively locking us into an endless payment cycle. This is not an increase; it is a forced, perpetual cost with no opt-out.  While I understand HP is unwilling to change its subscription model, what I am asking is whether HP intends to honor the original purchase agreements for customers like us who made their investment before this shift.

column124: Da diverso tempo, tutti noi operatori abbiamo noatao un netto  calo della qualità dei consumabili per hp indigo serie 3. In particolare, la durata media è notevolmente dimunita in alcuni stock più frequentemente(PIP e BLANKET), con un impatto diretto sulla produttività e sulla gestione operativa. Inoltre, riscontriamo spesso che i ricambi che ci vengono forniti sono rigenerati, ma in modo approssimativo, con prestazioni inferiori rispetto  alle standard atteso. In diversi casi, i pezzi non sono nemmeno disponibili e dobbiamo attendere tempi di consegna non compatibili con la continuità produttiva.  Tutto questo avviene, purtroppo, a nostro discapito: quando i consumabili non raggiungono il life span previsto, rischiamo di ricevere note di debito a fine mese, perché non rientriamo nei parametri HP di durata attesa. Questa situazione risulta penalizzante per chi, come noi, lavora con serietà e attenzione, ma si trova a dover gestire materiali di qualità inferiore senza averne alcuna responsabilità.  A questo si aggiunge un’altra criticità importante: i tempi di spedizione dei consumabili. Attendere 8–10 giorni lavorativi per ricevere dei materiali oggi appare del tutto fuori scala rispetto agli standard logistici attuali. Oggi, con una logistica efficiente, si riesce a spedire merce in tutta Europa in meno di tre/quattro giorni. Questo ritardo ci costringe a pianificare approvvigionamenti con ampio anticipo, e quando si verificano urgenze o imprevisti, il sistema semplicemente non regge
column125: For some time now, all of us operators have noticed a sharp decline in the quality of consumables for HP Indigo Series 3. In particular, the average life has significantly decreased in some stocks more frequently (PIP and BLANKET), with a direct impact on productivity and operational management. Furthermore, we often find that the spare parts supplied to us are regenerated, but in an approximate way, with lower performance than the expected standard. In several cases, the parts are not even available and we have to wait for delivery times that are not compatible with production continuity.  Unfortunately, all of this happens to our detriment: when the consumables do not reach the expected life span, we risk receiving debit notes at the end of the month, because we do not fall within the HP parameters of expected life. This situation is penalizing for those who, like us, work seriously and carefully, but find themselves having to manage lower quality materials without having any responsibility for it.  Added to this is another important criticality: the shipping times of the consumables. Waiting 8–10 working days to receive materials today seems completely out of scale with current logistics standards. Today, with efficient logistics, we can ship goods throughout Europe in less than three/four days. This delay forces us to plan supplies well in advance, and when emergencies or unforeseen events occur, the system simply cannot cope

column124: This survey may seem a little brutal, but it is my honest reflection of how we feel about the organization at this point.  I feel like this is a "safe space" to share these details, while we still beat the HP drum to the public.  We rely more on HP Indigo today than at any time in our company history.  We are continuing to purchase more presses as we expand our locations.  It is vital to the success of our company that HP do everything in their power to support us in those endeavors.  Press uptime and print quality are of paramount importance. With the 1-day SLAs that we are expected to execute, we cannot have a press down and reprints are extremely costly and time consuming.   I feel that HP has taken advantage of users with the new SaaS structures. Services we rely on that were included with press purchases are now being charging for them at an exponential rate.  The best example of this is the Creativity Power Pack.  We used to purchase a SmartStream license for our site for approximately $3500.  Now I have to pay $100 per user, per month.  By the time I have all users on boarded, that cost will be north of $1000 per month and over $13000 per year. Just some honest feedback.  Happy to hop on a call to discuss any or all of these items. Thanks, Brian Scott

column116: Seems to have gone down hill lately.   Availability of engineers being a key point. Very difficult to get hold of an engineer, and even harder to get access to one that is fully trained and understands our press fully. All too often issues go on and on for too long. Availability of parts is a huge issue. Often the things we need in order to continue running the press, for example a small 3D printed coupling on the top of the Ink Tank, isn't in the UTK - so we have to wait nearly 24 hours for a replacement part during which the machine is either down or not performing as it should. At the very least, more parts should be available in the UK for all UK Indigo users to have access to.  Also, we do not like how come August, HP will be charging for access to Print Beat, something that we've come to rely upon, and has been free since we first moved to B2 Indigo 7 years ago.   Finally, half the videos/tools in the Knowledge Zone are now hidden behind the Xr paywall. Again, when an operator needs access to information to keep the press up and running, we would expect these videos to be available to all, and not just to people who pay more.

column144: Would have rated the experience a 4, but an incident last month significantly impacted our confidence in the supplies system. The Cyan ink hadn't arrived with our monthly order due to 'low stock levels'. While we understand supply issues can occur, the more appropriate response would have been to send at least a box or two to tide us over. column128: The process of working with HP Industrial Print has been extremely difficult due to a lack of transparency, repeated delays, and poor communication. Some key challenges included:  We were not informed in advance that the try-and-buy offer required a full financial approval process for the 6-month deferral. This was brought up at the last minute, making it unnecessarily stressful to navigate.  Installation of the 200K press has been slow and inefficient, as one of the two assigned technicians is regularly pulled away mid-day, leaving just one person on-site.  We were not told that the 200K only comes with one L1 Delta training seat. We assumed we could send an operator as part of our regular training credits, but were later told we’d have to forfeit four existing seats — something that was never communicated in advance.  It took nearly a month for the contracts team to send finalized paperwork.  Finally, we received an unexpected invoice for not meeting the lifespan score on the 25K, despite recent praise from HP’s own solutions architect for our best practices. This is due to our high use of white ink for flexible packaging — something that impacts wear and is inherent to our business. When I asked for the charge to be waived, the response was simply, “This will be very difficult to reverse,” which shows a lack of accountability on HP’s part.  Taken together, this has made the entire process frustrating and disappointing.

column144: When we got our series 4, we trained ourselves not to waste any consumable as possible to the point of even filtering imaging oil to be reusable. But with regards to reusing blankets on our press, HP once allowed it, and with new updates, they are making it more and more difficult to do. As I said with our HP representatives we can extend the life of the blanket to more than 150% of its recommended lifespan simply by swapping blankets depending on the substrate size. HP should really really consider this practice as a way to be sustainable. There are some challenges with black market activities, but if you can make the serial number of the blanket bind to the press and no other press can use it, it can be a potential saving for HP. Which means people can run any size of substrate on the press without too much planning.  We admit that we don't run our press at its optimum operational efficiency thats why saving consumables is one of our biggest priority and a good performance indicator.

column124: Print OS qui devient payant… Les Malus/Bonus en fonction du % d'utilisation des consommables…  Pour rappel, notre métier est concepteur, fabricant d'étiquettes. Les statistiques de HP ne sont pas notre priorité.

column214: Organisation HP de plus en plus rigide. C'est un ressenti de plus en plus présent. Beaucoup moins de réactivité.  Notre partenariat avec HP a débuté il y a 20 ans. Le sens client était présent. On agissait très rapidement pour minimiser les arrêts machines.  Aujourd'hui, à chaque niveau (y compris dans l'organisation interne HP), il faut tout justifier 3 fois avant d'agir.  Les opérateurs, qui certains ont 20 ans d'expérience sur HP Indigo, remontent des problèmes à des personnes bilingues mais non qualifiées, qui à leur tour remontent les problèmes et suivent des procédures.  Cependant, rien à dire sur les différents interlocuteurs qui sont disponibles (Responsables, Ingénieurs, techniciens, assistance…)  Ils sont en première ligne, mais on sent parfois leur impuissance pour accélérer la procédure.  Le service n'est plus à la hauteur de ce qui faisait la force d'HP.
column215: HP's organization is becoming increasingly rigid. This is a growing perception. Much less responsiveness. Our partnership with HP began 20 years ago. Customer focus was present. We acted very quickly to minimize machine downtime. Today, at every level (including within HP's internal organization), everything must be justified three times before taking action. Operators, some of whom have 20 years of experience with HP Indigo, escalate problems to bilingual but unqualified people, who in turn escalate the problems and follow procedures. However, there's nothing to say about the various contacts available (managers, engineers, technicians, support staff, etc.). They are on the front lines, but we sometimes feel their powerlessness to speed up the process.  The service no longer lives up to HP's strengths.
